content: The study investigated the effects of supplementation in children using two different regimens. One group received an intervention supplement containing 14 micronutrients at twice the recommended dietary allowance (RDA), including 800 mcg/day of vitamin A. The other group received a standard supplement with one RDA of six micronutrients, including 400 mcg/day of vitamin A. After six months, all children were transitioned to the standard supplement. The primary outcome of interest was mortality at 12 months, with children stratified by antiretroviral (ARV) use. The intervention group showed slightly better anthropometric parameters compared to the control group, but baseline nutritional status was not analyzed. A recent Cochrane review on micronutrient supplementation in HIV-infected children and adults highlighted a lack of data on vitamin A supplementation in HIV-infected children. Five small trials included in the review provided strong evidence of clinical benefits of vitamin A supplementation on mortality in HIV-infected children, with moderate evidence for morbidity and growth benefits. Adverse effects were reported in isolated cases with small sample sizes. However, none of these studies specifically addressed HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), and thus they were excluded from this analysis. Vitamin A supplementation is currently recommended for children with SAM and those with HIV infection. However, there is no data to directly address whether HIV-infected children with SAM are more susceptible to adverse effects from vitamin A supplementation or would benefit from an adapted administration regimen compared to uninfected children with SAM. Until such data becomes available, it is recommended that HIV-infected children with SAM receive vitamin A supplements in the same manner as uninfected children. Acute diarrheal disease is the second leading cause of death among children worldwide, and HIV-infected children experience disproportionately high mortality during acute diarrheal episodes. HIV-infected children with SAM are at particularly high risk for opportunistic pathogens. Malabsorption during and after diarrheal episodes further complicates their recovery from SAM, hindering nutritional rehabilitation. The overall quality of data addressing therapeutic strategies for HIV-infected children with SAM and diarrhea is very low, as no prospective randomized trials have been conducted in this population. One randomized trial in Zambia compared an elemental diet to a standard nutritional rehabilitation diet in HIV-infected and uninfected children with persistent diarrhea and malnutrition. Both groups showed similar improvements in weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) and weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), but the elemental diet was associated with greater weight gain. However, the small sample size limits the generalizability of these findings. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in South Africa investigated short-term multiple micronutrient supplementation, including 300 mcg/day of vitamin A and 8 mg/day of zinc, in HIV-infected children hospitalized with diarrhea. The primary outcome was the duration of hospitalization, and no significant difference was observed between the placebo and supplementation groups. Both groups included fewer than 25 children, and no subgroup analysis was presented for malnourished children (WAZ < -2). Zinc supplementation has been shown to reduce the risk and severity of diarrhea and pneumonia in children without HIV infection. A placebo-controlled trial in HIV-infected children found that 10 mg/day of zinc for up to six months did not increase viral load but reduced the incidence of watery diarrhea. However, a subsequent study in 32 children did not show any benefit of prophylactic zinc supplementation on diarrheal morbidity. Zinc supplementation is recommended for children with SAM and diarrhea and is not considered unsafe for HIV-infected children. The optimal feeding regimens for HIV-infected children with SAM remain unclear. Two studies investigated recovery patterns in HIV-infected and uninfected children with SAM. One observational study found no significant difference in the duration of treatment phases between the two groups. A prospective cohort study found no significant difference in nutritional recovery among HIV-infected children who survived compared to uninfected children, although mortality was higher in the HIV-infected group. Trials of dietary supplements added to therapeutic feeds have not demonstrated significant differences in recovery rates. For example, an RCT in Burkina Faso investigated the addition of spirulina to the diet of HIV-infected and uninfected children with SAM but did not present statistical analysis of differences between treatment groups. Another RCT found no significant difference in nutritional cure rates among HIV-infected children with SAM given ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) with or without a symbiotic (prebiotic and probiotic) supplement. Although HIV-infected children who survive SAM may achieve similar growth parameters as uninfected children, mortality rates remain higher. Further research is needed to evaluate the effects of antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation in children with SAM, including optimal timing, pharmacokinetics, metabolic toxicities, and clinical outcomes such as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Studies should also assess the risks and benefits of vitamin A and zinc supplementation in HIV-infected children with SAM, including whether adapted administration regimens would be beneficial. Clinicians must continue to manage HIV-infected children with SAM despite the lack of high-quality evidence. General principles of medicine and clinical experience from other patient populations should guide management. Early initiation of ART in HIV-infected children has been associated with decreased mortality and improved growth outcomes. Concerns about potential ART toxicity in children with SAM are not supported by prospective data, and delaying ART initiation may result in poorer outcomes. Children with SAM who develop IRIS after ART initiation should be managed similarly to those without SAM, with treatment options including corticosteroids or modification of ART regimens. HIV-infected children are at high risk for diarrhea, which can be particularly problematic in those with SAM. Optimal gut integrity is crucial for nutritional rehabilitation. Clinicians should focus on timely assessment and management of dehydration, appropriate rehydration, and treatment of prolonged diarrhea. Nitazoxanide may be considered for cryptosporidium-related diarrhea, and prolonged diarrhea may warrant initiation of ART. Further research is needed to address these gaps in evidence and improve outcomes for this vulnerable population.
